short.headline: India's methane is rising, and coal mines are gaining on cattle
short.dek: A satellite-informed count puts India's methane at 35.96 million tonnes in 2024, third globally, with farming's share shrinking and fossil-fuel leaks growing fastest.
short.body: Methane traps over 80 times more heat than CO2 over 20 years. India's emissions reached 35.96 million tonnes in 2024, up from 31 million tonnes a decade ago. While cattle and rice paddies still dominate, their share fell from 75% to 70%. Coal mining and oil-and-gas operations now cause 11.9% of the total, up from 8.3%. Two independent estimates now agree within half a percent, and the biggest named sources are Coal India's opencast mines, not landfills.

macha.heading: Macha, what does all this methane data actually mean?
macha.body: Think of methane as the short, intense burst of a pressure cooker whistle versus the slow simmer of CO2. India's methane is rising, and most of it still comes from our cattle and paddy fields, which is what you'd expect. But here's the twist: the share of methane leaking from coal mines and gas fields is growing fastest. That's actually a bit of good news, because a leaky coal mine is a spot you can fix, unlike a cow burping in a field. Two different ways of measuring this gas now line up nicely, so we can trust the numbers more. The big coal mines are the hotspots you'd want to look at first, not the local landfill.
macha.soWhat: India has a methane problem, but the fastest-growing part of it comes from places we can actually plug.

article.title: How much methane is India actually releasing, and who is responsible for it?
article.standfirst: A satellite-informed database reveals India's methane emissions rose to 35.96 million tonnes in 2024. While livestock and rice fields still dominate, coal mines and gas fields are gaining share. Two independent counts now agree within half a percent.
article.bodyMarkdown:
## Is India's methane going up or down?

India's methane emissions are on a rising path. The latest estimate from Climate TRACE, a satellite-informed database, puts the country's methane at 35.96 million tonnes in 2024, up from 31 million tonnes in 2015. Methane is a greenhouse gas that packs a punch: over 20 years, it traps about 80 times more heat than carbon dioxide. But it breaks down in the atmosphere within a decade, so cutting it buys time faster than [cutting CO2](/articles/how-much-co2-does-india-emit/). Because methane warms the planet fast but fades quickly, reducing it now can slow warming sooner than an equivalent cut in CO2. The upward slope steepened slightly after 2020. This is just methane, not all [greenhouse gases](/articles/how-is-climate-change-changing-india/).

## Where does India rank among the world's biggest methane emitters?

India sits at third place among the selected large emitters in Climate TRACE's 2023 data. China towers over everyone at 83.02 million tonnes, followed by the United States at 38.31 million tonnes. India's 35.27 million tonnes are uncomfortably close to the US level. Russia (21.06 million tonnes), Brazil (19.42 million), and Indonesia (14.93 million) are further behind. China's lead is enormous because it has far more coal mining and rice cultivation. The US emits more from oil and gas, while India's profile is still mostly agricultural. The ranking is not an exhaustive global list, but it shows that a handful of countries dominate methane emissions.

## Who is responsible for most of India's methane?

Agriculture remains by far the largest source. In 2024, livestock and rice paddies together released 25.14 million tonnes of methane, accounting for 69.9% of India's total methane. Cows and buffaloes belch methane as they digest grass, a process called enteric fermentation. Flooded rice fields also produce methane when organic matter decomposes underwater. Enteric fermentation is a natural process that's hard to stop without changing diets or herd sizes. Similarly, flooded rice paddies create anaerobic conditions that microbes love, releasing methane bubbles. Waste (landfills and wastewater) contributes 4.94 million tonnes (13.7%), and fossil-fuel operations (coal mining, oil and gas) add 4.28 million tonnes (11.9%). Other sources make up the remaining 4.4%.

## Which sector is growing fastest?

The share of methane from fossil-fuel operations has risen the fastest. In 2015, coal mines and oil-and-gas fields contributed 8.3% of India's methane; by 2024, that share reached 11.9%. Agriculture's share slipped from 75% to 69.9%, even though its absolute emissions still grew from 23.26 million tonnes to 25.14 million tonnes. Waste also edged up slightly from 11.9% to 13.7%. [Coal mining in India](/articles/how-dependent-is-india-on-coal/) has expanded to meet power demand, and as mines get deeper, they release more trapped gas. Oil and gas operations, from aging pipelines to new gas fields, also leak methane during extraction and transport. The upshot: while cattle and rice still dominate the pie, the fastest growth is in point-source fossil methane, which is physically concentrated at mines and wells and therefore easier to capture.

## Can we name the biggest methane hotspots?

Yes, and they are almost all coal mines. Climate TRACE's asset-level data lists the top point sources in units of CO2 equivalent over 100 years (blended gases). The top two are not coal mines but giant onshore oil-and-gas producing regions: the Cambay basin (12.17 million tonnes CO2e) and the Assam region (9.09 million tonnes CO2e). After that, the list is dominated by opencast coal mines run by Coal India subsidiaries. Dipka coal mine in Chhattisgarh emits 3.58 million tonnes CO2e, followed by Nigahi, Dudhichua, Gevra, Kusmunda, and Lingaraj. These are all state-owned. Refineries were excluded because their emissions are mostly CO2 from combustion, not methane leaks.

## What about the landfills we hear about?

Landfills are often in the news, but individually they are much smaller sources than the coal mines. The top waste methane site is the landfill at Majura Taluka in Surat, at 5,81,252 tonnes CO2e. Ahmedabad's Pirana follows at 5,51,775 tonnes, and Delhi's Ghazipur at 4,86,405 tonnes. Others include Perugundi, Bhalaswa, and Dhapa. While these sites are significant locally, they are dwarfed by the fossil-fuel point sources. Landfill methane estimates carry high uncertainty because gas generation depends on organic waste composition, how sealed the site is, and local climate, unlike well-mapped coal mines.

## Do two different ways of counting India's methane agree?

They now do, and that convergence is the most reassuring finding in this data. Climate TRACE, built from satellite observations and bottom-up accounting, and Climate Watch, a modelled reconstruction that fills gaps between official reports, are two independent estimates. In 2015, Climate TRACE reported 31 million tonnes while Climate Watch reported 33.21 million tonnes, a gap of 6.7%. By 2023, the two were nearly identical: Climate TRACE 35.27 million tonnes versus Climate Watch 35.13 million tonnes, a difference of just 0.4%. Two different methods landing close makes both more credible. It shows both approaches are homing in on a consistent estimate, giving confidence that the numbers are roughly right.

## What about agriculture methane specifically?

The two estimates broadly agree on agriculture, though the gap between them is wider and bumpier than in the other sectors. Climate TRACE consistently reports higher agriculture methane: in 2023, it was 25.1 million tonnes versus Climate Watch's 23.53 million tonnes, a difference of 6.7%. That offset has ranged from about 3.5% to 8.6% over the years, with no clear upward or downward trend. A persistent gap like this usually reflects a methodological difference, such as different emission factors for livestock or rice, rather than a growing error. Both agree on the rising trend.

## Does fossil-fuel methane check out?

The agreement on fossil-fuel methane is the tightest of all. In 2015, Climate TRACE gave 2.56 million tonnes while Climate Watch gave 3.48 million tonnes, a discrepancy of 26.5%. By 2023, the two were essentially the same: Climate TRACE 3.72 million tonnes, Climate Watch 3.7 million tonnes, a gap of just 0.5%. This means the fastest-growing component of India's methane emissions is now verified by two independent methods. It's a strong signal that coal-mine and oil-gas methane are real and rising.

## How to read these numbers

Climate TRACE uses satellite-informed, bottom-up models to estimate emissions for each facility and sector. It is not a direct reading from a methane sensor; it is an informed calculation. Climate Watch's figure is a separate modelled reconstruction from CAIT and PIK, built to fill the years between countries' sparse official submissions. Both are estimates, not measurements. The asset-level data is reported in CO2e over 100 years, blending methane with other gases, so the hotspot ranking is a ranking of climate impact, not pure methane tonnage. India's own official Biennial Update Reports (BUR-3 for 2016, submitted 2021; BUR-4 for 2020, submitted December 2024) are snapshots years apart, not a time series, which is common for non-Annex I countries. Climate Watch lacks a separate waste sector series for India, so no second independent estimate exists to check Climate TRACE's landfill-and-wastewater figure. That is a genuine open question.

editorialPlan.heroDescription: India's methane emissions have risen steadily, hitting 35.96 million tonnes in 2024 per Climate TRACE, making it the world's third-largest methane emitter. Agriculture remains the biggest source, but fossil-fuel operations are growing fastest. A comparison with Climate Watch shows convergence, boosting confidence. Named point sources are overwhelmingly coal mines.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Methane is a greenhouse gas that traps about 80 times more heat than CO2 over 20 years, but it breaks down in the atmosphere within a decade. It comes from cattle, rice paddies, landfills, and leaks from coal mines and oil/gas wells.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: The entire article is about methane specifically, not all greenhouse gases.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A way to bundle different greenhouse gases into one number by converting them to the amount of CO2 that would cause the same warming. Usually based on a 100-year time horizon (GWP100).
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Point-source rankings use CO2e 100yr, so they mix gases; we must explain that it's not just methane.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Leaks of greenhouse gases from industrial activities, like methane escaping from a coal seam or a gas pipeline joint. They are not from burning fuel but from the extraction and handling process.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Climate Watch reports 'fugitive emissions', which compares to Climate TRACE's fossil-fuel operations sector.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A global database that uses satellites, sensors, and modelling to estimate emissions from individual facilities and sectors. It is built by a coalition of research groups and nonprofits.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: This is the primary data source for India's methane estimates in the article.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A platform that hosts historical emissions data compiled by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) and the Climate Analysis Indicators Tool (CAIT). It fills gaps between countries' official reports to create a complete time series.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Used as the second independent estimate to compare against Climate TRACE.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: The digestive process in ruminant livestock (cows, buffaloes, goats) that produces methane as a by‑product, exhaled or belched.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: This is the single largest source of India's agricultural methane.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: Methane trapped in coal seams that is released when mining disturbs the seam. Opencast mines can vent huge quantities.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Most of India's top point sources are coal mines; capturing CMM is a practical mitigation option.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A report that developing countries submit every two years to the UNFCCC, detailing their national greenhouse gas inventories and mitigation actions. Non‑Annex I countries like India have flexibility in submission timing.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India's official methane figures come from these snapshots, but they are years apart and not a continuous series.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A single, identifiable location that emits pollution, like a coal mine, a landfill, or an oil refinery. It's the opposite of 'diffuse' sources like cattle spread across a landscape.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Fossil-fuel methane's rise matters because point sources are easier to fix than millions of cows.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change. The international treaty under which countries report their greenhouse gas emissions and negotiate climate action.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: India's Biennial Update Reports are submitted under this framework; sparse reporting is structural, not a sign of hidden data.

glossaryBlocks.plainMeaning: A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps compared to CO2 over a specific period, usually 20 or 100 years. Methane's high GWP20 is why cutting it now can quickly slow warming.
glossaryBlocks.whyItMattersHere: Point-source values in CO2e depend on the GWP chosen, usually 100-year, which understates methane's immediate punch.

visualizationDecisions.reason: Annual data from 2015-2024 shows the full trend clearly on a phone screen; line with sparse bars avoids clutter.
A horizontal bar chart with one bar per country, sorted descending, is instantly readable for country comparisons.
A 100% stacked bar or a donut shows sector shares at a glance, ideal for composition.
Overlapping lines for sector shares over time clearly reveal relative growth; a single line for fossil-fuel share rising stands out.
Ranked horizontal bars with names make the list of point sources scannable and compelling.
Same reasoning as above, focusing on waste sites for immediate recognition.
Two lines with faint shading between them shows convergence dramatically.
Similar to total reconciliation, showing the consistent offset.
Dual lines that start apart and end nearly overlapping tell a compelling convergence story.

chartExplainers.title: India's methane is rising, not falling
chartExplainers.takeaway: India's methane emissions climbed from 31 million tonnes in 2015 to 35.96 million tonnes in 2024, a steady rise.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart plots annual methane emissions from 2015 to 2024, based on Climate TRACE data. Methane (CH4) is a potent greenhouse gas that warms the atmosphere about 80 times more than CO2 over a 20-year period. The line rises almost every year, with a steeper climb after 2020. The total reached 35.96 million tonnes in 2024. This is not the full greenhouse gas picture — it includes only methane, not CO2 or N2O.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Before any breakdown, the headline trend: is India's methane going up or down.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the line climb from 31 million tonnes in 2015 to 35.96 million in 2024. The slope steepens slightly after 2020.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't mistake a single-year dip for a trend; the overall direction is clearly upward.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a clean line chart with sparse axis labels and horizontal gridlines.

chartExplainers.title: India is the world's third-biggest methane emitter
chartExplainers.takeaway: In 2023, India emitted 35.27 million tonnes of methane, placing it third behind China (83.02 million tonnes) and the United States (38.31 million tonnes).
chartExplainers.detail: This horizontal bar chart compares methane emissions for selected large countries in 2023, sourced from Climate TRACE. China dominates with 83.02 million tonnes, well ahead of second-place United States at 38.31 million tonnes. India is close behind the US at 35.27 million tonnes. Russia (21.06 Mt), Brazil (19.42 Mt), and Indonesia (14.93 Mt) are lower. The ranking is not an exhaustive global list but highlights the heavyweights.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Scale means little without company: where does India actually sit next to the other big emitters.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Compare the bar lengths: China far ahead at 83 Mt, then the US at 38 Mt, India at 35 Mt. After that, Russia, Brazil, Indonesia are smaller.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read it as an exhaustive global rank; it shows only selected major emitters.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with country names and emissions right-aligned ensure readability on a phone.

chartExplainers.title: Livestock and rice still dominate, but their share is shrinking
chartExplainers.takeaway: Agriculture (livestock and rice) accounted for 69.9% of India's methane in 2024, down from 75% in 2015.
chartExplainers.detail: A stacked area or donut chart shows the sectoral composition for the latest year. Agriculture, primarily enteric fermentation in cattle and flooded rice paddies, is still by far the largest source at 25.14 million tonnes. Waste contributes 13.7% and fossil-fuel operations 11.9%. A small 'other' slice completes the picture. While agriculture dominates, its share has been slowly eroding.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Solutions depend on the source: a cattle-and-rice problem needs different fixes than a coal-mine or landfill problem.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Look at the stacked segments: the largest chunk (nearly 70%) is agriculture; waste and fossil fuel are the two smaller but growing slices.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume the share shift means agricultural methane is falling in absolute terms; it is rising too, just slower.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A donut chart or a single stacked bar works well; label the largest segments clearly.

chartExplainers.title: Fossil-fuel methane's share has grown fastest
chartExplainers.takeaway: Fossil-fuel operations' share jumped from 8.3% in 2015 to 11.9% in 2024, while agriculture's share fell from 75% to 69.9%.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart traces the annual percentage share of three sectors over a decade. Agriculture (solid line) drifts downward, waste (dashed) edges up slightly, but fossil-fuel operations (dotted) climb sharply. Fossil fuel methane, mostly from coal mines and oil-and-gas fields, grew from 2.56 million tonnes in 2015 to 4.28 million tonnes in 2024. That's a 67% rise in absolute terms, making it the fastest-growing category. Because such leaks are point sources, they are often easier to capture than diffuse agricultural emissions.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: A composition snapshot hides which slice is actually growing fastest — and it isn't agriculture.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Watch the fossil-fuel line rise from 8.3% in 2015 to 11.9% in 2024, while agriculture flattens and then dips.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't think of it as a bad thing; this shift means point-source emissions are becoming more prominent, which may be easier to tackle.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A multi-line chart with three distinct colours and a legend placed above avoids clutter.

chartExplainers.title: India's named methane hotspots are almost all coal mines
chartExplainers.takeaway: The top two point sources are large onshore oil-and-gas regions, but the next eight are all opencast coal mines run by Coal India subsidiaries.
chartExplainers.detail: This ranked bar chart lists the 15 largest named point sources according to Climate TRACE asset-level data, expressed in tonnes of CO2 equivalent (100-year GWP). The Cambay conventional onshore region tops at 12.17 million tonnes CO2e, followed by the Assam region at 9.09 million tonnes. From third place downwards, the list is dominated by coal mines: Dipka (3.58 Mt), Nigahi (2.86 Mt), Dudhichua (2.86 Mt), Gevra (2.62 Mt), and others. All are held by Coal India subsidiaries. Refineries were deliberately excluded because their emissions are mostly combustion CO2, not fugitive methane. The blended CO2e unit means the ranking reflects overall climate impact, not raw methane tonnage.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Sector totals are abstract; naming the actual sites makes the story concrete.
chartExplainers.howToRead: The top two are broad onshore oil-and-gas regions. Then eight coal mines, led by Dipka and Gevra. All are Coal India subsidiaries.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: The unit is CO2e 100yr, not raw methane; this mixes in some CO2 from fuel use. Also, this ranking deliberately excludes refineries.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Horizontal bars with site names and owners beneath each bar keep it readable; use abbreviations for owners if needed.

chartExplainers.title: The landfills you'd actually recognise
chartExplainers.takeaway: Delhi's Ghazipur and Ahmedabad's Pirana are among the top waste methane sites, each emitting less than 600,000 tonnes CO2e — far smaller than major coal mines.
chartExplainers.detail: This chart isolates the top 10 landfill and wastewater methane sources. The Majura Taluka landfill in Surat leads at 581,252 tonnes CO2e. Pirana (Ahmedabad) follows at 551,775 tonnes, and Ghazipur (Delhi) at 486,405 tonnes. Other familiar names include Perugundi, Bhalaswa, and Dhapa. These sites are individually small compared to coal mines in the combined ranking, but they represent the locally visible face of India's waste methane. Landfill estimates are uncertain because methane generation varies with rainfall, temperature, and waste composition.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Landfills rarely crack a combined ranking against coal mines by raw tonnage, but Ghazipur and Pirana are the household names of India's waste-methane problem and deserve their own frame.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Majura Taluka (Surat) tops the waste list at ~581 kt CO2e, followed by Pirana (Ahmedabad), Ghazipur (Delhi), and others from major cities.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: These values are in CO2e, not methane alone; and they are smaller than the coal mine sources on the combined list.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A table-like bar chart with location names and values works; group by city for context.

chartExplainers.title: Two different ways of counting India's methane now roughly agree
chartExplainers.takeaway: Climate TRACE and Climate Watch, two independent estimates, started 6.7% apart in 2015 but converged to just 0.4% difference by 2023.
chartExplainers.detail: A dual-line chart with light shading between them shows the convergence. In 2015, Climate TRACE reported 31 million tonnes while Climate Watch gave 33.21 million tonnes (a gap of -6.7%). Over nine years, the two lines draw together. By 2023, Climate TRACE estimated 35.27 million tonnes and Climate Watch 35.13 million tonnes, a difference of only 0.14 million tonnes. This convergence between a satellite-informed bottom-up method and a modelled gap-fill reconstruction builds mutual credibility. It suggests that despite their different approaches, they are capturing a consistent picture of India's methane emissions.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: One estimate alone invites doubt. Does a second, differently-built one land anywhere close?
chartExplainers.howToRead: Two lines: Climate TRACE (solid) and Climate Watch (dashed). In 2015, they were 31 vs 33.21; by 2023, they are 35.27 vs 35.13, a gap of just 0.14 Mt.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't claim one is 'right' and the other 'wrong'; convergence between independent methods is what makes both credible.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Use a clean line chart with a subtle shaded band; add small data labels on the key endpoints.

chartExplainers.title: Agriculture methane: the two estimates track closely
chartExplainers.takeaway: Climate TRACE consistently reports higher agriculture methane than Climate Watch, by a margin that fluctuates between about 3.5% and 8.6% with no clear trend.
chartExplainers.detail: This line chart compares agriculture-specific methane estimates. Climate TRACE's line runs about 0.8 to 1.9 million tonnes above Climate Watch's line each year. In 2023, the figures were 25.1 million tonnes versus 23.53 million tonnes, a gap of 6.7%. This percentage has fluctuated between roughly 3.5% and 8.6% over the recorded period, without a clear trend. A persistent but non-trending gap usually points to a systematic methodological difference — for example, different assumptions about how much methane each cow produces or how much is emitted per hectare of paddy — rather than a problem that is getting worse. Both agree on the upward trend.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Agriculture is the biggest slice, so it is the most important sector to see cross-checked.
chartExplainers.howToRead: Climate TRACE consistently higher (roughly 0.8-1.9 Mt, 3.5-8.6% above Climate Watch), but the gap fluctuates without trending wider or narrower.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: A fluctuating but non-trending gap is a methodology offset, not evidence one is wrong; it means they are tracking the same underlying trend.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: Keep the two lines distinct (solid vs dashed) and annotate the annual gap with small text or arrow.

chartExplainers.title: Fossil-fuel methane: the smallest gap of all
chartExplainers.takeaway: Climate TRACE and Climate Watch now agree almost perfectly on fossil-fuel methane, with a gap of only 0.5% in 2023, down from 26.5% in 2015.
chartExplainers.detail: In 2015, the two estimates were far apart: Climate TRACE reported 2.56 million tonnes while Climate Watch gave 3.48 million tonnes. The 0.92 million tonne gap (Climate TRACE lower) amounted to a 26.5% difference. Over the following years, Climate TRACE's numbers rose more steeply, while Climate Watch's remained relatively flat. By 2023, they nearly met: Climate TRACE 3.72 million tonnes versus Climate Watch 3.7 million tonnes. This 0.02 million tonne gap (0.5%) is the smallest of any sector. The tight agreement on fugitive emissions from coal, oil, and gas gives strong confidence that the rise in fossil methane is real, not an artefact of one model.
chartExplainers.whyShowThis: Coal-mine and oil-and-gas fugitive methane is the sector growing fastest in share — worth checking it isn't an artifact of one model.
chartExplainers.howToRead: In 2015, the gap was 0.92 Mt (Climate TRACE lower). By 2023, it's 0.02 Mt, a near-perfect match.
chartExplainers.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read this as proof of zero error; both models have uncertainties. But their agreement on fossil fuel is remarkably tight.
chartExplainers.mobileNote: A dual-line chart with a vertical line at 2023 and a callout 'gap 0.5%' drives the point home.

editorialPlanDraft.answerThesis: India's methane emissions reached about 36 million tonnes in 2024, rising from 31 million tonnes in 2015, with agriculture still the largest source but fossil-fuel operations growing fastest; two independent estimates now converge within 0.4%, spotlighting coal mines as concentrated and actionable point sources.
requiredConcepts: Scale and rank, stated plainly: Climate TRACE puts India's all-sector methane at roughly 31 million tonnes in 2015, climbing to about 35-36 million tonnes by 2023-2024 - a rising line. Among the world's largest emitters, India ranks third in 2023, behind China (by a wide margin) and the United States, and ahead of Russia, Brazil and Indonesia. State this as one estimate's ranking among a handful of the largest emitters, not an exhaustive global league table

Methane in plain English, defined on first use: it is a much more potent but much shorter-lived greenhouse gas than carbon dioxide, trapping far more heat per tonne over the next two decades before breaking down in the atmosphere within about a decade, versus CO2 which lingers for centuries. This is why cutting methane now has an outsized near-term cooling effect compared to an equivalent cut in CO2 - it is the fastest lever available for slowing warming in this decade specifically, not a substitute for cutting CO2 long-term

Composition, and the shift inside it: agriculture (mainly livestock digestion and rice paddies) is by far the largest source of India's methane, but its share slipped from around 75% in 2015 to about 71% in 2023. Fossil-fuel operations (coal mining, oil and gas) grew fastest, rising from roughly 8% to over 10% of the total over the same years; waste (landfills and wastewater) also crept up a little. State both the absolute dominance of agriculture and the relative shift away from it

Named places, honestly framed: the top named point sources are overwhelmingly opencast coal mines operated by Coal India Limited's subsidiaries (state-run coalfields companies such as South Eastern Coalfields, Northern Coalfields, Central Coalfields, Eastern Coalfields, Mahanadi Coalfields and Bharat Coking Coal), alongside two large onshore oil-and-gas producing regions. Because asset-level Climate TRACE data reports a single blended co2e_100yr figure rather than separate gases, this ranking is a point-source climate-impact ranking, not a pure-methane one - oil refineries were deliberately excluded from it because their emissions are mostly combustion CO2, not fugitive methane. Named landfills and wastewater sites (including Surat's Majura Taluka site, Ahmedabad's Pirana and Delhi's own Ghazipur landfill) are individually smaller than the big coal mines and get their own separate top-10 list so they are not lost in the combined ranking

The reconciliation, which is the article's most important honest finding: Climate TRACE (satellite-informed, largely bottom-up per-source) and Climate Watch (a separately modelled reconstruction with CAIT/PIK lineage) are two independently built ways of estimating India's methane. Nationally, they started about 7% apart in 2015 (Climate TRACE running lower) and had converged to within roughly half a percent of each other by 2023. Agriculture shows a small, fairly stable gap across the whole period (Climate TRACE running a few percent above Climate Watch), consistent with a steady methodology offset rather than a fast-moving real divergence. Fossil-fuel methane (Climate TRACE) versus fugitive emissions (Climate Watch) tracks closest of all. Frame convergence between two independently built estimates as what makes both more credible, not as one 'catching' the other in an error

The honest gap that remains: Climate Watch has no equivalent 'waste' sector series for India, so there is no second independent estimate to check Climate TRACE's landfill-and-wastewater methane figure against. India's own Biennial Update Reports to the UNFCCC (BUR-3, covering 2016 data, submitted February 2021; BUR-4, covering 2020 data, submitted December 2024) are the official position, but they are snapshots years apart, not a running series, which is a structural feature of how non-Annex-I countries report under the UNFCCC, not evidence of concealment. Present the waste-sector comparison as the one genuinely open question in this data, not a settled scandal

Why fossil-fuel methane's rising share is the most actionable finding: unlike diffuse agricultural methane spread across millions of farms and animals, fugitive methane from a named coal mine or gas field is physically concentrated at a point source, which is exactly what makes it feasible to capture, flare, or monetise (e.g. coal-mine methane drainage projects) in a way that livestock methane is not. That is the practical 'so what' behind the composition shift, not a policy prescription

Number discipline is absolute: every statistic must come from the evidence packet's actual chart data, never invented or recalled with false precision. Use rounded, spoken forms ('roughly 35 million tonnes', 'about a third') rather than decimal precision, except where the evidence packet's locked numbers specify an exact displayValue. Keep the macha layer warm and plain-spoken, with any wit in the headings, not the explanations. No em-dashes

sectionPlan.heading: Is India's methane going up or down?
sectionPlan.job: Show the headline trend: India's all-sector methane emissions from 2015 to 2024, rising from 31 million tonnes to 35.96 million tonnes. Explain methane's warming potency and why the direction matters.
conceptsToExplain: Methane's short-lived but strong warming effect
Climate TRACE as a satellite-informed estimate
sectionPlan.caveat: Data is for methane only, not all greenhouse gases; 2024 is the latest estimate.

sectionPlan.heading: Where does India rank among the world's biggest methane emitters?
sectionPlan.job: Place India's 35.27 million tonnes (2023) in global context: third after China and the US, ahead of Russia, Brazil, Indonesia. Emphasize China's large lead and India's proximity to the US level.
sectionPlan.caveat: Ranking is based on Climate TRACE data for selected large emitters, not an exhaustive global list.

sectionPlan.heading: Who is responsible for most of India's methane?
sectionPlan.job: Break down the latest sectoral composition: agriculture 69.9%, waste 13.7%, fossil-fuel operations 11.9%, other 4.4%. Explain livestock and rice dominance.
conceptsToExplain: Sectoral sources: enteric fermentation, rice paddies, landfills, coal mining
sectionPlan.caveat: Based on Climate TRACE's classification; 'other' includes small sources not broken out.

sectionPlan.heading: Which sector is growing fastest?
sectionPlan.job: Show the composition shift 2015-2024: agriculture share fell from 75% to 69.9%, fossil-fuel share rose from 8.3% to 11.9%. Highlight fossil-fuel operations growth.
sectionPlan.caveat: Absolute emissions rose in all sectors; agriculture still dominates in volume.

sectionPlan.heading: Can we name the biggest methane hotspots?
sectionPlan.job: Reveal the top 15 point sources (CO2e 100yr): two onshore oil-and-gas regions and then coal mines. Explain that this is a blended ranking, not pure methane, and refineries excluded.
sectionPlan.caveat: Values are in CO2e 100yr, thus include some CO2 and N2O; not exactly methane tonnage.

sectionPlan.heading: What about the landfills we hear about?
sectionPlan.job: Show separate top-10 waste methane sources: Ghazipur, Pirana, etc. Note they are smaller than coal mines and deserve their own ranking.
sectionPlan.caveat: Landfill estimates are highly uncertain; organic waste decay depends on site conditions.

sectionPlan.heading: Do two different ways of counting India's methane agree?
sectionPlan.job: Compare Climate TRACE vs Climate Watch total methane: gap narrowed from -6.7% in 2015 to +0.4% in 2023. Explain convergence builds trust.
sectionPlan.caveat: Both are estimates, not direct measurements; the convergence is reassuring but not proof.

sectionPlan.heading: What about agriculture methane specifically?
sectionPlan.job: Agriculture methane gap: Climate TRACE 25.1 Mt vs Climate Watch 23.53 Mt in 2023, gap ~6.7%. Note the stable offset, not a growing divergence.
sectionPlan.caveat: Climate TRACE consistently higher; offset likely arises from different emission factors or activity data.

sectionPlan.heading: Does fossil-fuel methane check out?
sectionPlan.job: Fossil methane gap: 3.72 vs 3.70 Mt in 2023, gap only 0.5%, the closest of all sectors. From -26.5% in 2015, showing dramatic convergence.
conceptsToExplain: Convergence of bottom-up and modelled approaches
sectionPlan.caveat: Climate Watch measures 'fugitive emissions', which may not exactly match Climate TRACE's 'fossil-fuel operations'; still, the agreement is striking.

sectionPlan.heading: How to read these numbers
sectionPlan.job: Explain the methods: Climate TRACE (satellite-informed, bottom-up) vs Climate Watch (modelled gap-fill). Note CO2e blending in asset-level data. Mention India's official BURs are sparse, lagged snapshots, and no second estimate for waste. State these facts plainly, not as accusations.
sectionPlan.caveat: This section does not have a companion chart; it is a methodological grounding for the whole article.

chartPlan.title: India's methane is rising, not falling
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Before any breakdown, the headline trend: is India's methane going up or down.
chartPlan.howToRead: Watch the line climb from 31 million tonnes in 2015 to 35.96 million in 2024. The slope steepens slightly after 2020.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't mistake a single-year dip for a trend; the overall direction is clearly upward.

chartPlan.title: India is the world's third-biggest methane emitter
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Scale means little without company: where does India actually sit next to the other big emitters.
chartPlan.howToRead: Compare the bar lengths: China far ahead at 83 Mt, then the US at 38 Mt, India at 35 Mt. After that, Russia, Brazil, Indonesia are smaller.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read it as an exhaustive global rank; it shows only selected major emitters.

chartPlan.title: Livestock and rice still dominate, but their share is shrinking
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Solutions depend on the source: a cattle-and-rice problem needs different fixes than a coal-mine or landfill problem.
chartPlan.howToRead: Look at the stacked segments: the largest chunk (nearly 70%) is agriculture; waste and fossil fuel are the two smaller but growing slices.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't assume the share shift means agricultural methane is falling in absolute terms; it is rising too, just slower.

chartPlan.title: Fossil-fuel methane's share has grown fastest
chartPlan.whyShowThis: A composition snapshot hides which slice is actually growing fastest - and it isn't agriculture.
chartPlan.howToRead: Watch the fossil-fuel line rise from 8.3% in 2015 to 11.9% in 2024, while agriculture flatens and then dips.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't think of it as a bad thing; this shift means point-source emissions are becoming more prominent, which may be easier to tackle.

chartPlan.title: India's named methane hotspots are almost all coal mines
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Sector totals are abstract; naming the actual sites makes the story concrete.
chartPlan.howToRead: The top two are broad onshore oil-and-gas regions. Then eight coal mines, led by Dipka and Gevra. All are Coal India subsidiaries.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: The unit is CO2e 100yr, not raw methane; this mixes in some CO2 from fuel use. Also, this ranking deliberately excludes refineries.

chartPlan.title: The landfills you'd actually recognise
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Landfills rarely crack a combined ranking against coal mines by raw tonnage, but Ghazipur and Pirana are the household names of India's waste-methane problem and deserve their own frame.
chartPlan.howToRead: Majura Taluka (Surat) tops the waste list at ~581 kt CO2e, followed by Pirana (Ahmedabad), Ghazipur (Delhi), and others from major cities.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: These values are in CO2e, not methane alone; and they are smaller than the coal mine sources on the combined list.

chartPlan.title: Two different ways of counting India's methane now roughly agree
chartPlan.whyShowThis: One estimate alone invites doubt. Does a second, differently-built one land anywhere close?
chartPlan.howToRead: Two lines: Climate TRACE (solid) and Climate Watch (dashed). In 2015, they were 31 vs 33.21; by 2023, they are 35.27 vs 35.13, a gap of just 0.14 Mt.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't claim one is 'right' and the other 'wrong'; convergence between independent methods is what makes both credible.

chartPlan.title: Agriculture methane: the two estimates track closely
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Agriculture is the biggest slice, so it is the most important sector to see cross-checked.
chartPlan.howToRead: Climate TRACE consistently higher (roughly 0.8-1.9 Mt, 3.5-8.6% above Climate Watch), but the gap fluctuates without trending wider or narrower.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: A fluctuating but non-trending gap is a methodology offset, not evidence one is wrong; it means they are tracking the same underlying trend.

chartPlan.title: Fossil-fuel methane: the smallest gap of all
chartPlan.whyShowThis: Coal-mine and oil-and-gas fugitive methane is the sector growing fastest in share - worth checking it isn't an artifact of one model.
chartPlan.howToRead: In 2015, the gap was 0.92 Mt (Climate TRACE lower). By 2023, it's 0.02 Mt, a near-perfect match.
chartPlan.mistakeToAvoid: Don't read this as proof of zero error; both models have uncertainties. But their agreement on fossil fuel is remarkably tight.

visualizationDecisions.reason: Annual data from 2015-2024 shows the full trend clearly on a phone screen; line with sparse bars avoids clutter.
A horizontal bar chart with one bar per country, sorted descending, is instantly readable for country comparisons.
A 100% stacked bar or a donut shows sector shares at a glance, ideal for composition.
Overlapping lines for sector shares over time clearly reveal relative growth; a single line for fossil-fuel share rising stands out.
Ranked horizontal bars with names make the list of point sources scannable and compelling.
Same reasoning as above, focusing on waste sites for immediate recognition.
Two lines with faint shading between them shows convergence dramatically.
Similar to total reconciliation, showing the consistent offset.
Dual lines that start apart and end nearly overlapping tell a compelling convergence story.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Methane is a greenhouse gas that traps about 80 times more heat than CO2 over 20 years, but it breaks down in the atmosphere within a decade. It comes from cattle, rice paddies, landfills, and leaks from coal mines and oil/gas wells.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The entire article is about methane specifically, not all greenhouse gases.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A way to bundle different greenhouse gases into one number by converting them to the amount of CO2 that would cause the same warming. Usually based on a 100-year time horizon (GWP100).
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Point-source rankings use CO2e 100yr, so they mix gases; we must explain that it's not just methane.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Leaks of greenhouse gases from industrial activities, like methane escaping from a coal seam or a gas pipeline joint. They are not from burning fuel but from the extraction and handling process.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Climate Watch reports 'fugitive emissions', which compares to Climate TRACE's fossil-fuel operations sector.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A global database that uses satellites, sensors, and modelling to estimate emissions from individual facilities and sectors. It is built by a coalition of research groups and nonprofits.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: This is the primary data source for India's methane estimates in the article.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A platform that hosts historical emissions data compiled by the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) and the Climate Analysis Indicators Tool (CAIT). It fills gaps between countries' official reports to create a complete time series.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Used as the second independent estimate to compare against Climate TRACE.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps compared to CO2 over a specific time period, usually 20 years (GWP20) or 100 years (GWP100).
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Methane's GWP is why it is so potent in the short term; CO2e values depend on the chosen GWP.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A single, identifiable location that emits pollution, like a coal mine, a landfill, or an oil refinery.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The top-sources chart names specific point sources; fossil-fuel methane's rise matters because point sources are easier to plug than diffuse agricultural sources.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: Methane trapped in coal seams that is released when mining disturbs the seam. Opencast mines can vent huge quantities.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: Most of India's top point sources are coal mines; capturing CMM is a practical mitigation option.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The digestive process in ruminant livestock (cows, buffaloes, goats) that produces methane as a by-product, exhaled or belched.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: This is the single largest source of India's agricultural methane.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: A report that developing countries submit every two years to the UNFCCC, detailing their national greenhouse gas inventories and mitigation actions. Non-Annex I countries like India have flexibility in submission timing.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: India's official methane figures come from these snapshots, but they are years apart and not a continuous series.

glossaryPlan.plainMeaning: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, the international treaty under which countries report their emissions and negotiate climate action.
glossaryPlan.whyItMattersHere: The BURs are submitted under this framework; the sparseness of reporting is structural, not a sign of hidden data.

proseRules: No calculations unless the evidence packet supplies the derived number

selectionRules: Start from the page question, not from the indicator name.
Choose the smallest set of visuals that explains scale, trend, structure, comparison, and caveat.
Prefer mobile-friendly charts: line charts with sparse ticks, horizontal bars, share strips, pyramids only when essential, and no dense tables.
Use one strong pull quote only when the evidence supports it with a number.
Add glossary blocks for technical terms that normal readers may not know.
caveats: Use only figures present in lockedNumbers or sourceSummaries.
If a related theme indicator is present, you may use it for context, but do not pretend it is the main answer.
If source coverage is thin, say so directly.
Do not compare states, districts, or cities unless the evidence packet contains those geographies.
forbiddenClaims: Do not infer causality from a trend unless the evidence explicitly supports it.
Do not cite a source that is not present in sourceSummaries.
